column22: 2026-05-29 10:40:00;geetha.nallamada;Fair challenge. It is worth it because every consumer downstream writes its joins against the shape, and retrofitting valid_from into thirty existing queries is the expensive version. But I have written honestly in the header that the history is not real yet, so nobody builds a tier-at-time-of-purchase analysis on it and gets a confidently wrong answer. Real change capture is PULSE-119.
column23: 2026-06-05 15:15:00;divya.maram;Built, and the header says exactly that. Accepted.

column5:
As the business
I want daily and monthly sales marts
So that the recurring questions are answered without touching the facts.

Acceptance criteria
* 031_mart_sales_daily.sql and 032_mart_sales_monthly.sql
* revenue, orders, units, AOV, gross profit, margin percent
* AOV computed at header grain from fact_orders, per PULSE-25 and PULSE-50
* daily mart reconciles to fact_orders - reconciliation check two
* period-over-period and year-over-year comparisons using dim_date keys
column21: 2026-06-01 11:40:00;geetha.nallamada;First mart, and the first place the AOV grain trap can actually bite. See PULSE-56 - it bit.
column22: 2026-06-05 16:25:00;divya.maram;Reconciliation check two is green and the daily mart matches the fact across the full range.

column4: AOV reported 40% low - averaged from the line fact
column5:
Observed: AOV in the first draft of mart_sales_daily reads about 40% below the
figure finance calculates by hand.

Impact: none published - caught before the mart was released. Had it shipped,
it would have been quoted in the monthly review and would have looked entirely
plausible.

Cause: AOV was computed as AVG(net_amount) over fact_sales, which is line
grain. It is the average line value, not the average order value.

Fix: compute from fact_orders at header grain, per the definition written in
PULSE-25 in March. Add a quality check comparing mart AOV against a header
grain recomputation.
column21: 2026-06-01 11:50:00;divya.maram;Spotted it because the number looked low against what finance quotes, not because anything failed. Which is exactly what PULSE-25 said would happen - there is no error for averaging the wrong grain.
column22: 2026-06-01 12:20:00;geetha.nallamada;We wrote the warning down in March and then walked straight into it in June. I am not treating that as a failure of the documentation - the document is how Divya knew to be suspicious. But it is the argument for the check, because documentation does not run nightly.
column23: 2026-06-02 09:35:00;devendranath.singam;Adding my vote for the check. Two explicit facts (PULSE-50) made the mistake possible to detect; only an assertion makes it impossible to ship.
column24: 2026-06-04 12:25:00;geetha.nallamada;Fixed and the check is in. Retro item: any metric with a grain judgement in its definition gets an assertion when it is first implemented, not when it first goes wrong.

column4: Streamlit shell and the data access layer
column5:
As a stakeholder
I want one application with a page per subject area
So that I am not sent five different links.

Acceptance criteria
* dashboards/streamlit/app.py with multipage navigation
* dashboards/streamlit/data_access.py is the only module that talks to the
  warehouse - no page issues its own SQL
* query results cached with a documented TTL
* the as-of date from gold.analysis_window shown on every page
column21: 2026-06-10 10:30:00;divya.maram;One data access module rather than SQL scattered through the pages. When a definition changes there is exactly one place to change it, and the pages stay about presentation.
column22: 2026-06-17 16:05:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted. The as-of date on every page is not optional - if the platform's today is not the calendar's today, the page has to say so out loud.

column5:
As a reader of these dashboards
I want every chart to follow the same visual rules
So that I can read a new chart without relearning what the colours mean.

Rules
* one palette, defined once, colour-blind safe, legible in light and dark
* one hue per entity, consistent across every page - a region is the same
  colour everywhere
* fixed categorical order, never sorted by value between renders
* sequential ramps for magnitude only, diverging only around a real midpoint
* no dual axes, ever
* direct labelling in preference to legends where the series count allows
column21: 2026-06-09 11:15:00;geetha.nallamada;Doing this before the first chart rather than after the thirtieth. Retrofitting consistency across a built estate is an order of magnitude more expensive, and half of it never gets done.
column22: 2026-06-12 14:20:00;divya.maram;Fixed categorical order caught something already. A bar chart sorted by value redrew in a different order between two refreshes and I misread the change as a data problem for about ten minutes.
column23: 2026-06-18 15:25:00;geetha.nallamada;Merged. The no-dual-axis rule is the one I expect to be argued with most, and PULSE-59 records why it holds.

column4: ADR-004: No dual axes, fixed categorical order
column5:
Decision: charts in this platform never use a secondary y-axis, and
categorical series keep a fixed declared order rather than sorting by value.

Rationale for no dual axes: the crossing point of two series on independent
scales is an artefact of the scales chosen, and readers consistently read it
as a real event. Where two measures must be compared, use two aligned charts
or index both to a common base.

Rationale for fixed order: a chart that reorders between renders makes change
detection unreliable, and a reader who has learned a layout should be able to
keep using it.

Cost accepted: some comparisons need two charts where one would have fit.
column21: 2026-06-15 11:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Written up with the alternatives, so that when someone wants revenue and margin on one chart there is a documented answer rather than a debate.

column5:
As a category manager
I want product-level performance in one mart
So that assortment decisions do not need bespoke SQL each time.

Acceptance criteria
* 033_mart_product_performance.sql at product and month grain
* revenue, units, margin, return rate, rank within category
* contribution to category revenue, and a Pareto position
* built on fact_sales at line grain, which is the correct grain here
column21: 2026-06-16 10:50:00;divya.maram;Line grain is right for this one, and I have said so in the header. After PULSE-56 I would rather every mart state which fact it is built on and why.
column22: 2026-06-19 14:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted. That header convention should apply to all marts - please add it to the ones already built when you next touch them.

column4: Prepare QA onboarding - access, environment and runbook
column5:
Get everything in place before the QA analyst starts on 15 Jun, so that day
one is doing the job rather than raising access tickets.

Checklist
* Jira, Confluence, GitHub and Slack access requested
* dev warehouse read role approved
* a written runbook: clone, venv, generate data, build warehouse, run tests,
  run the dashboards
* first-week goals agreed and written down
column21: 2026-06-09 09:30:00;devendranath.singam;Access requests are in. GitHub and Slack are instant; the warehouse read role needs the data owner and that took nine days for Divya, so it is raised now.
column22: 2026-06-12 15:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Runbook written and dry-run by Deven from a clean machine. First-week goal is deliberately narrow: build the warehouse, run the suite, and write down what is not covered.

column5:
First week for the QA analyst joining 15 Jun 2026.

* environment up and warehouse built locally
* full pipeline and quality suite run end to end
* walkthrough of the medallion layers, the KPI contract and the four ADRs
* produce a written gap analysis: what the current tests do not cover
column21: 2026-06-15 14:20:00;neha.chauhan;Environment is up and the warehouse built on the second attempt - the first failed because I had not run the generator first. Worth one line in the runbook, since it is the kind of thing that is obvious once you know it.
column22: 2026-06-17 11:40:00;neha.chauhan;Read through the KPI document and the ADRs. The thing that stands out is that most of the past bugs were silent rather than loud, so my gap analysis is going to be mostly about assertions between layers rather than more unit tests.
column23: 2026-06-19 16:25:00;neha.chauhan;Gap analysis written. Three areas with no coverage at all: the dashboards, the analytics modules, and anything asserting that ops tables survive a rebuild. The third one worries me most because a rebuild is routine.
column24: 2026-06-19 16:45:00;geetha.nallamada;That third point is a good instinct and it is now PULSE-86. Welcome aboard.

column4: Test strategy and regression scope by layer
column5:
As the team
I want a written statement of what is tested at each layer
So that "covered" means something specific rather than a count of tests.

Acceptance criteria
* per layer - bronze, silver, gold, marts, analytics, dashboards, streaming -
  what is asserted, what is deliberately not, and why
* the difference between the quality suite and the test suite stated plainly
* the regression pack per layer identified, and gaps listed as tickets
column21: 2026-06-17 10:10:00;neha.chauhan;Drawing the line as: the quality suite asserts things about the data on every run; the test suite asserts things about the code on every push. Both matter and they are not substitutes, which is not obvious from the outside.
column22: 2026-06-18 14:30:00;divya.maram;That distinction is clearer than how we had been describing it internally. Worth putting in the README rather than only in the strategy doc.
column23: 2026-06-19 15:35:00;geetha.nallamada;Approved.

column5:
As an executive
I want revenue, margin, orders and growth on one page
So that the monthly review starts from an agreed number.

Acceptance criteria
* headline tiles: revenue, gross margin percent, orders, AOV, each with a
  period-over-period comparison
* revenue trend with a prior-year comparison series
* top and bottom performing categories and regions
* every tile traceable to a definition in the KPI document
* as-of date visible
column21: 2026-06-25 11:20:00;geetha.nallamada;Every tile links to its definition. If someone disagrees with a number, the argument should start at the definition rather than at the chart.
column22: 2026-07-01 10:15:00;neha.chauhan;Tested against a hand-computed set from the generated data. All tiles match. One note: the period-over-period comparison on the first day of a month compares against a single day, which is technically correct and reads as a 90% collapse.
column23: 2026-07-02 15:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Good catch. Added a partial-period label to the comparison rather than hiding it - the reader needs to know the period is incomplete, not be protected from it.

column5:
As a sales manager
I want to explore sales by product, region, channel and time
So that I can answer my own questions without raising a request.

Acceptance criteria
* filters: date range, region, channel, category
* trend, breakdown by dimension, product table with sortable measures
* drill from category to product
* filters reflected in every chart on the page, with the active filter set
  stated in plain language
column21: 2026-06-29 14:40:00;divya.maram;Stating the active filters in a sentence at the top of the page. Screenshots of filtered dashboards get pasted into decks with no indication of what was filtered, and then argued about.
column22: 2026-07-02 11:05:00;neha.chauhan;Filter combinations tested including the empty result case, which previously rendered an empty chart with no explanation. Now shows a message saying no data matches.
column23: 2026-07-03 15:25:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column4: Dual-axis chart on the sales page
column5:
Observed: the revenue-and-margin chart on the sales page uses a secondary
y-axis, against ADR-004.

Impact: the two series cross in September in the demo data. The crossing point
is an artefact of the two scales and reads as a real event.

Fix: split into two aligned charts sharing an x-axis.
column21: 2026-06-30 10:25:00;neha.chauhan;Raising this from ADR-004 rather than from taste. The ADR says never, and reviewing against a written rule is much easier than reviewing against an opinion.
column22: 2026-06-30 11:40:00;divya.maram;Guilty - it was the quickest way to get both series in one place and I talked myself into it. Splitting into two aligned charts.
column23: 2026-07-02 14:05:00;geetha.nallamada;Fixed and verified. This is the ADR earning its keep in a code review, which is exactly what it is for.

column5:
As a regional manager
I want regional and store performance in one mart
So that comparisons between stores are consistent.

Acceptance criteria
* 038_mart_regional_store.sql at region, store and month grain
* revenue in reporting and local currency
* like-for-like comparison excluding stores open less than 13 months, with
  the exclusion count exposed rather than silent
column21: 2026-06-26 10:30:00;divya.maram;Like-for-like exposes how many stores were excluded and why. A like-for-like number without that count is an unfalsifiable claim.
column22: 2026-07-01 15:15:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted, and local currency alongside reporting currency as agreed in PULSE-34.

column5:
As the team
I want automated checks that every page renders and its numbers match the
warehouse
So that a mart change cannot silently break a page.

Acceptance criteria
* tests/test_dashboards.py imports each page and exercises its data functions
* headline tile values asserted against a direct warehouse query
* runs in CI
* a broken page fails the build
column21: 2026-06-29 11:50:00;neha.chauhan;Asserting the tile values against a direct query rather than only that the page renders. A page that renders confidently wrong numbers is worse than one that crashes.
column22: 2026-07-03 16:05:00;divya.maram;Merged and green. It caught a stale column reference on the sales page during development, which is the first time a dashboard bug has been caught by CI rather than by a person.

column4: Executive page 4x slower after the region filter landed
column5:
Observed: executive page load went from about 1.1s to 4.6s on the largest
preset after the region filter was added.

Cause: the filter was applied in Python after loading the full unfiltered
result set, and the cache key did not include the filter values, so every
filter change was a cache miss on a full scan.

Fix: push the filter into SQL, include filter values in the cache key.
column21: 2026-06-29 15:15:00;neha.chauhan;Noticed on the largest preset, which is why it is worth testing against something bigger than the demo set. On the demo data it is imperceptible.
column22: 2026-07-02 11:15:00;devendranath.singam;Filter pushed into SQL, cache key fixed. Back to 0.9s, slightly better than before because the filtered query touches less data.

column5:
As the executive page
I want a purpose-built mart
So that headline tiles are one small read rather than several large ones.

Acceptance criteria
* 041_mart_executive.sql, pre-aggregated to the tile grain
* period-over-period and year-over-year precomputed
* reconciles to mart_sales_daily, added as a reconciliation check
column21: 2026-07-03 14:35:00;geetha.nallamada;Reconciliation against the daily mart added, so a pre-aggregation that drifts from its source fails the build rather than quietly disagreeing with the sales page.

column5:
As the business
I want one row per customer with their full commercial picture
So that customer questions have a single starting point.

Acceptance criteria
* 034_mart_customer_360.sql, one row per customer
* first and last order date, lifetime orders, lifetime revenue, average order
  value at header grain, tenure, recency, preferred category and channel
* recency anchored to gold.analysis_window
* customers with no orders present, not filtered out
column21: 2026-07-08 10:20:00;geetha.nallamada;Zero-order customers stay in. They are the denominator of activation, and filtering them here is how activation problems become invisible - see PULSE-74, which is the same mistake in a different costume.
column22: 2026-07-15 15:35:00;divya.maram;Accepted. Every recency column reads analysis_window, verified by the CURRENT_DATE test.

column5:
As marketing
I want customers scored and segmented on recency, frequency and monetary value
So that campaigns can target behaviour rather than guesswork.

Acceptance criteria
* 035_mart_rfm_segments.sql with quintile scores on each axis
* named segments - Champions, Loyal, At Risk, Hibernating, Lost, New
* segment boundaries defined in the KPI document, not only in SQL
* recency anchored to analysis_window
* segment sizes stable between runs on the same data
column21: 2026-07-10 11:30:00;divya.maram;Quintiles over the active customer base rather than fixed thresholds, so the segmentation stays meaningful as the business grows. Documented, because it means a customer can change segment without changing behaviour if the base shifts around them.
column22: 2026-07-14 09:45:00;neha.chauhan;Ran the segmentation twice on the same dataset and got identical sizes. That is only true because of the analysis window - worth a regression test, so I have put it in the customer pack.
column23: 2026-07-16 15:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted, and the boundary definitions are in the KPI document.

column5:
As the business
I want monthly acquisition cohorts and their retention curves
So that we can see whether retention is improving.

Acceptance criteria
* 036_mart_cohort_retention.sql at cohort month and period number grain
* cohort defined by first purchase month - see PULSE-74
* retention as active customers in period divided by cohort size
* the same dataset produces the same curve on every run
column21: 2026-07-13 14:20:00;geetha.nallamada;First version was built on signup month and produced a retention cliff at month one that nobody could explain. See PULSE-74.
column22: 2026-07-17 15:05:00;divya.maram;Rebuilt on first purchase month. The curve is now smooth and, more importantly, it is stable across runs.

column4: Cohorts defined on signup month show an activation problem as churn
column5:
Observed: cohorts built on signup month show a retention cliff of roughly 60%
between period 0 and period 1.

Diagnosis: it is not a retention problem. A large share of signups never
purchase at all, so they enter a cohort and leave it without ever having been
a customer. The cliff is the activation rate wearing a retention costume, and
it was about to be presented to the board as a retention crisis.

Fix: define a cohort by the month of first purchase, so cohort membership
means "became a customer". Activation is a separate metric, defined
separately, and it is a real problem worth its own workstream.
column21: 2026-07-13 14:50:00;divya.maram;This is the second time a definition choice has produced a plausible and completely misleading picture. The first was AOV. Both were caught by someone thinking the number looked odd rather than by anything automated.
column22: 2026-07-14 09:20:00;geetha.nallamada;Right, and I do not think that is fully fixable with assertions - a definition can be internally consistent and still answer the wrong question. What we can do is require every cohort-shaped metric to state its membership rule on the chart itself, so a reader can catch what a test cannot.
column23: 2026-07-14 15:30:00;neha.chauhan;I can assert the mechanical part: cohort size must equal the count of customers whose first order falls in that month. That catches a regression even if it cannot catch a bad definition.
column24: 2026-07-16 11:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Both done. And the activation finding goes to the business as a finding rather than being quietly absorbed into a definition change - it is genuinely the more useful discovery of the two.

column5:
As retention
I want a monthly churn view with a stated definition
So that churn is measurable and arguable on the definition rather than the
number.

Acceptance criteria
* churn defined for a non-contractual business: no purchase within the
  customer's expected repurchase window, defined per segment
* the definition and its judgement calls written into the KPI document
* monthly churned count, churn rate and revenue at risk
* anchored to analysis_window
column21: 2026-07-09 10:40:00;divya.maram;Churn in a non-contractual setting is a judgement, not an observation. Nobody cancels - they just stop. Writing the window rule down with its arbitrariness admitted rather than presenting it as measured fact.
column22: 2026-07-17 16:15:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted. Per-segment windows rather than one global window, since a weekly-grocery customer and an annual-electronics customer are not comparable on a single threshold.

column5:
As marketing
I want customer lifetime value by cohort and channel
So that acquisition spend can be judged against what a customer is worth.

Acceptance criteria
* analytics/customer/clv.py with an explainable formula: average order value,
  purchase frequency, expected lifespan, margin
* cumulative realised value curves by cohort, not only a projected figure
* the projection horizon stated and the assumption labelled on the chart
column21: 2026-07-10 11:20:00;geetha.nallamada;An explainable formula over a fitted probabilistic model. Marketing has to defend an acquisition budget with this number, and a number they cannot explain is a number they cannot defend.
column22: 2026-07-15 10:30:00;divya.maram;Realised curves alongside the projection, which is the honest version - the projection is an assumption and the realised curve is a measurement, and they should not look alike on a chart.
column23: 2026-07-17 14:45:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column4: Regression pack for the customer marts
column5:
Regression coverage for customer_360, RFM, cohort retention and churn.

Assertions
* customer_360 row count equals distinct customers in the dimension
* RFM segment sizes sum to the active customer count
* cohort size equals distinct customers whose first order is in that month
* every recency metric changes when analysis_window moves, and not otherwise
* two consecutive runs on the same data produce identical output
column21: 2026-07-14 15:35:00;neha.chauhan;The determinism assertion is the one I care most about. It is the property that makes every other test meaningful, and it is invisible until it breaks.
column22: 2026-07-17 16:35:00;geetha.nallamada;Agreed and accepted. That assertion is effectively a test of ADR-002 rather than of any one mart.

column5:
As marketing and retention
I want the customer analytics on one page
So that segments, cohorts and value are read together.

Acceptance criteria
* RFM segment overview with sizes and revenue contribution
* cohort retention heatmap using a sequential ramp, magnitude only
* CLV curves by cohort, projection visually distinct from realised
* churn trend with the definition stated on the page
* segment membership rule visible on the cohort chart, per PULSE-74
column21: 2026-07-24 11:15:00;divya.maram;Sequential ramp on the heatmap, single hue. Retention is a magnitude, and a diverging palette here would invent a midpoint that does not exist.
column22: 2026-07-29 10:20:00;neha.chauhan;Verified every figure on the page against the marts. Also checked the empty-segment case, which now renders a labelled empty state rather than a blank panel.
column23: 2026-07-30 15:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column4: Event bus abstraction with two implementations
column5:
As the platform
I want one bus interface with a file-based and a Kafka implementation
So that streaming can be developed and tested without a broker.

Acceptance criteria
* streaming/bus.py defines publish, subscribe and commit
* NDJSON file implementation for local development and CI
* Kafka/Redpanda implementation for the deployed path
* the same consumer code runs against both, unmodified
* offsets persisted per consumer group in both implementations
column21: 2026-07-22 10:30:00;devendranath.singam;One interface, two implementations. Without the file implementation, CI needs a broker and every test becomes slow and flaky, and the streaming layer ends up as the untested corner of the platform.
column22: 2026-07-28 14:10:00;neha.chauhan;This is the difference between me being able to test the streaming path and not. Running the consumer against files in CI is exactly the same code path as against Redpanda.
column23: 2026-07-30 16:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column4: Four correlated event topics and the producer
column5:
As the platform
I want a producer emitting correlated orders, payments, inventory and
clickstream events
So that the real-time layer can be built and tested against realistic traffic.

Acceptance criteria
* streaming/events.py defines the schemas with an explicit event_time
* correlation is real - a payment event references an order event that exists,
  an inventory movement follows a sale
* configurable rate, and a burst mode for load testing
* a replayable seeded mode producing an identical stream
column21: 2026-07-24 15:40:00;devendranath.singam;Correlation matters as much here as in the batch generator. Uncorrelated events make the funnel and the payment success rate meaningless, and both are the metrics this layer exists to serve.
column22: 2026-07-31 15:25:00;divya.maram;Replay mode is what makes the KPI assertions possible - same seed, same stream, same numbers.

column5:
Add Redpanda to docker-compose so the Kafka path is exercised locally with the
same code that will run deployed.

Acceptance criteria
* single-node Redpanda alongside Postgres
* topics created on startup
* documented switch between the file bus and the Kafka bus by environment
  variable only
column21: 2026-07-28 14:25:00;devendranath.singam;Redpanda rather than full Kafka for local - Kafka API compatible, one container, no ZooKeeper. The deployed target is Event Hubs, which speaks the same protocol.

column4: Micro-batched consumer with offsets committed after write
column5:
As the platform
I want a consumer that commits offsets only after a successful write
So that a crash loses no events.

Acceptance criteria
* micro-batches by count or time window, whichever comes first
* offset committed only after the batch is written and the transaction commits
* at-least-once delivery, with idempotent writes keyed on event id
* a crash mid-batch is tested and reprocesses without duplicating
column21: 2026-07-27 11:20:00;devendranath.singam;At-least-once with idempotent writes rather than chasing exactly-once. Exactly-once here would mean a distributed transaction across the broker and the warehouse for a KPI window that recomputes anyway.
column22: 2026-07-30 15:10:00;neha.chauhan;Wrote the crash test - kill the consumer mid-batch, restart, assert no duplicates and no gaps. It passes, and it failed the first time against an earlier build where the commit came first, so the test is doing real work.
column23: 2026-07-31 16:35:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column5:
All real-time KPI windows are computed on event_time carried in the event, not
on the time the consumer processed it.

Rationale: a replayed stream must reproduce exactly the KPIs it produced live.
Wall-clock windowing makes the real-time layer untestable, because the answer
depends on when you ran it.

Acceptance criteria
* every window derives from event_time
* late-arriving events assigned to their true window within a stated
  allowed-lateness bound, and counted when they fall outside it
* a replay test asserts identical KPIs from an identical stream
column21: 2026-07-23 09:50:00;devendranath.singam;This is ADR-002 applied to the streaming layer. Same principle, same reason: anchor to the data, not to the clock.
column22: 2026-07-31 16:58:00;neha.chauhan;Replay test asserts identical KPI output across two runs of the same seeded stream. Green.

column5:
As the platform
I want landed stream events and a recomputed KPI window in the warehouse
So that real-time metrics are queried the same way as batch metrics.

Acceptance criteria
* ops.stream_events as the landing table, with event id, type, event_time,
  ingest time and payload
* ops.realtime_kpis holding the current window, recomputed per micro-batch
* every KPI defined in SQL, not in the consumer - see the epic
* real-time revenue reconciles to batch revenue for a closed period
column21: 2026-08-05 10:15:00;devendranath.singam;The consumer lands events and triggers a recompute. It does not know what revenue means, and it must not - that is the only way one definition survives two pipelines.
column22: 2026-08-12 15:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Reconciliation between the real-time window and the batch fact for a closed day is green. That check is the proof the two pipelines agree.

column4: Batch rebuild silently wipes the streaming landing zone
column5:
Observed: after a routine full warehouse rebuild, ops.stream_events was empty
and the real-time dashboard showed zeros. No error anywhere.

Impact: about four hours of landed events lost. In a deployed system this is a
3am page and a hole in the record that nothing can reconstruct.

Cause: ops tables were created alongside the bronze tables using DROP TABLE IF
EXISTS followed by CREATE TABLE. The batch rebuild therefore dropped and
recreated the streaming landing zone as a side effect.

Fix
* ops.* tables use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and are never dropped by a
  pipeline stage
* ops DDL moved out of the bronze init path entirely
* a test asserts that a full batch rebuild leaves ops.stream_events row counts
  unchanged
column21: 2026-08-06 09:45:00;divya.maram;Real-time page was showing zeros this morning. I had run a full rebuild last night to pick up the new mart. Everything looked healthy - the rebuild succeeded, the quality suite passed, and four hours of events were simply gone.
column22: 2026-08-06 10:30:00;devendranath.singam;Found it. ops tables were being created in the same file as the bronze tables with DROP and CREATE. A batch job that can destroy the streaming layer is exactly the kind of coupling that causes a 3am page, and it has been sitting there since PULSE-22 in March.
column23: 2026-08-06 11:15:00;geetha.nallamada;This one goes in the retro properly. Both destructive DDL and cross-layer coupling, and neither the quality suite nor the test suite could see it because both only look at the warehouse after a successful build.
column24: 2026-08-06 14:20:00;neha.chauhan;This is the gap I flagged on my first week - nothing asserts that ops tables survive a rebuild (PULSE-86). Writing that test now, and it fails against the current main, which is what I wanted to confirm.
column25: 2026-08-11 15:15:00;devendranath.singam;Fixed. ops DDL is out of the bronze path, everything is IF NOT EXISTS, and Neha's test is green. Also grepped the whole repo for DROP TABLE - two other places, both in test teardown, both fine.

column4: Test that a batch rebuild cannot destroy the ops schema
column5:
Assert the isolation between the batch and streaming layers.

Assertions
* land events, run a full batch rebuild, assert ops.stream_events row count is
  unchanged
* same for ops.realtime_kpis, ops.pipeline_runs and ops.data_quality_results
* no pipeline stage issues DROP against the ops schema, asserted by scanning
  the DDL
column21: 2026-08-07 10:20:00;neha.chauhan;The DDL scan is worth having alongside the behavioural test. The behavioural test catches it happening; the scan catches someone reintroducing the pattern in a file that is not yet wired in.
column22: 2026-08-11 14:35:00;devendranath.singam;Both green. Between this and the CURRENT_DATE scan we now have two structural assertions that catch a whole class of mistake rather than one instance of it.

column5:
As operations
I want a live view of orders, payments, inventory movement and site activity
So that a gateway degradation is visible within minutes rather than the next
morning.

Acceptance criteria
* current-window KPIs: orders per minute, revenue rate, payment success rate,
  active sessions
* auto-refresh with the last update time and the window shown
* payment success rate against its recent baseline, so a drop is legible
* explicit indication when the stream is stale rather than showing an old
  number as if it were current
column21: 2026-08-10 11:30:00;divya.maram;The staleness indicator is the important part. A real-time dashboard silently showing a fifteen-minute-old number is worse than one that says the feed is down, because people act on it.
column22: 2026-08-13 14:15:00;neha.chauhan;Tested by stopping the producer. The page flags stale after the configured threshold and stops presenting the window as current.
column23: 2026-08-14 16:25:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted. This closes the original problem statement - Friday evening gateway degradation is now visible in minutes.

column5:
As another system
I want to read current real-time KPIs over an API
So that the dashboard is not the only way to consume them.

Acceptance criteria
* streaming/processors/realtime_api.py exposes the current window
* reads ops.realtime_kpis - it does not recompute anything
* window and last-update timestamp included in every response
* stale window returns a clear staleness indicator rather than an old value
column21: 2026-08-13 15:35:00;devendranath.singam;Reads the same table the dashboard reads. A second consumer that recomputes is a second definition, and we have been strict about that everywhere else.

column5:
As operations
I want funnel conversion and payment performance in one mart
So that drop-off and payment failure are analysed together.

Acceptance criteria
* 040_mart_funnel_payments.sql
* funnel stages from session through view, cart, checkout to purchase
* payment success rate on both denominators, labelled
* failure reasons broken down by gateway and method
column21: 2026-08-11 10:40:00;divya.maram;Both payment success denominators appear on the page with their labels, per PULSE-30. One number here would get quoted in the gateway negotiation and be the wrong one.
column22: 2026-08-14 15:05:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column5:
As marketing
I want campaign and channel performance with spend, revenue and ROAS
So that budget conversations start from a shared table.

Acceptance criteria
* 037_mart_marketing.sql building both marts
* spend, impressions, clicks, sessions, orders, revenue, ROAS, CPA
* the attribution basis of every revenue column named in the column name
  itself, not only in documentation
* unattributed revenue shown as its own line rather than distributed
column21: 2026-08-19 10:30:00;geetha.nallamada;Attribution basis goes in the column name - revenue_last_touch, not revenue. A column called revenue in a marketing mart is a lie by omission, because it is always attributed somehow.
column22: 2026-08-21 14:20:00;divya.maram;Unattributed revenue as its own line, currently 34% of the total. Distributing it proportionally would have hidden the single most important caveat about this whole mart.
column23: 2026-08-26 15:55:00;geetha.nallamada;Accepted.

column4: Publish five attribution models side by side
column5:
As marketing
I want the same revenue attributed five ways, presented together
So that budget decisions account for the uncertainty rather than ignoring it.

Models: first touch, last touch, linear, time decay, position based.

Acceptance criteria
* analytics/marketing/attribution.py computes all five over the same events
* output is one table, one row per channel, one column per model
* an upper_funnel_bias measure: first-touch credit minus last-touch credit,
  which identifies channels that a last-touch budget will systematically
  starve
* no default model, and no blended number anywhere in the output
column21: 2026-08-18 11:15:00;geetha.nallamada;No model here is correct. Publishing one would be a confident answer to a question we cannot answer, and it would immediately become the number - so we publish five and make the spread the finding.
column22: 2026-08-24 15:30:00;divya.maram;The spread is the finding. One influencer channel comes out at 1.8x ROAS on last touch and 6.1x on first touch. It has been having its budget cut for two quarters on the last-touch figure.

column4: Churn model scores 0.94 AUC - target leakage in the feature snapshot
column5:
Observed: the first churn model reported 0.94 AUC on a held-out set.

Diagnosis: leakage. Features were computed at the same moment as the label, so
recency_days effectively was the label - a customer is labelled churned
because they have not purchased recently, and the model was given exactly that
as a feature.

Impact: none published. Had it shipped, it would have scored beautifully and
predicted nothing, and the retention team would have received a list of
customers who had already left.

Fix: rewind the feature snapshot 90 days before the label window, so features
describe what was knowable at scoring time. Honest AUC is 0.71.
column21: 2026-09-03 10:35:00;divya.maram;Raising this against my own work. 0.94 on a churn model built in an afternoon is not a good sign, it is a symptom.
column22: 2026-09-03 11:40:00;geetha.nallamada;Correct instinct and worth saying plainly: a model that scores far better than the problem is hard is nearly always answering an easier question than the one you asked.
column23: 2026-09-04 09:30:00;neha.chauhan;Adding a temporal validation assertion to the analytics pack - the maximum feature timestamp must be earlier than the label window start. It is mechanical, but this class of bug is subtle to spot and trivial to assert.
column24: 2026-09-07 15:05:00;divya.maram;Fixed with a 90-day rewind. 0.71 AUC and it actually predicts. Neha's assertion is in and passing.

column4: ADR-005: Linear churn model over gradient boosting
column5:
Decision: use logistic regression for churn propensity, not the
gradient-boosted model that scored slightly better.

Rationale: the retention team has to know why a customer is at risk in order
to write a campaign to them. A ranked list from a black box tells them who but
not what to say. The coefficients are part of the deliverable.

Measured cost: about 0.03 AUC.

Revisit when: an action exists that needs only the ranking and not the reason.

column5:
Decision: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as the warehouse
engine, not Synapse.

Rationale: Synapse is the right answer past roughly a terabyte. Below that it
is a large bill for a warehouse that a single well-indexed relational database
serves faster. Current gold layer is under 40GB at the largest preset.

Migration path kept open: the gold layer is already a star schema, so moving
to a distributed engine is a DDL change and a bulk copy rather than a
remodelling exercise. A real path, kept open, not taken prematurely.

Revisit when: gold exceeds roughly 500GB, or concurrent query load degrades
p95 dashboard latency beyond 3s.

Establish and enforce that no .pbix binary is committed.

Rationale: a binary that cannot be diffed, reviewed or merged does not belong
in version control, and one that is three commits stale is worse than none at
all - people open it and trust it.

Acceptance criteria
* .gitignore excludes *.pbix
* a CI check fails the build if one is added
* the DAX library and the export script are the reviewable artefacts
* the reasoning documented for whoever tries to commit one next

column4: Wrap the pipeline in a real orchestrator

column5:
Route quality failures and pipeline errors to a person who is expected to
respond.

Why it has waited: Terraform creates the action group; nothing routes to it,

needed: an agreed rota, an agreed response expectation, and an agreed
definition of what is worth waking someone for.

Technical work once that exists: roughly two days.

column4: Geo holdout to replace the incrementality proxy

upswing, and it is labelled as such on the dashboard.

Why it has waited: it needs marketing to agree to withhold spend in selected
markets. That is a commercial conversation, not a sprint.

column4: Semantic layer to collapse the metric implementations
column5:
Collapse the metric implementations into one definition consumed by every
tool.

Current state: definitions live in one document and four implementations -
SQL marts, Python analytics, the real-time KPI window, and DAX. The
reconciliation checks keep the SQL side honest; the DAX side is verified by
hand.

Why it has waited: with three consumers the reconciliation checks were
sufficient. The DAX library (PULSE-110) makes it four, and hand verification
does not scale past that.

Trigger: a fifth consumer, or the first DAX-versus-SQL discrepancy that
